newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS - S.Africa sells Telkom stake for $1.26 bln.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - S.Africa sells Telkom stake for $1.26 bln.

text.p: South Africa clinched Sub-Saharan Africa's big privatisation deal on Wednesday, selling a 30 percent stake in state utility Telkom to a U.S.-Malaysian consortium for $1.261 billion.
SBC Communications Inc will pay 60 percent of the bill and Telekom Malaysia Bhd 40 percent.
The deal, the first major sell-off of state assets in South Africa and the largest direct investment in the country to date, values Telkom at $4.2 billion.
Of the proceeds, $1 billion will be injected back into Telkom to help fund its infrastructure expansion programme and the balance will go to the state to cut government debt.

Posts, Telecommunications and Broadcasting Minister Jay Naidoo said the partial privatisation would provide badly-needed capital, expertise and technology to enable Telkom to overcome the legacy of the apartheid era.
Millions of mainly black South Africans have no access to a telephone while affluent, white suburbs enjoy first world standards of service.
"The restructuring of Telkom will provide universal access to telephony services and an information backbone for macroeconomic development," Naidoo said.
"Telkom will at the same time be transformed into a world-class operator."

Telkom and its strategic equity partners -- who will enjoy a five-year exclusivity period in fixed line telephony -- have committed themselves to one of the fastest roll-out programmes in the world, promising to deliver 2.8 million new lines including 120,000 payphones over the next five years.
Telkom is committed to a $12 billion or 53 billion rand capital expenditure programme over a five-year period, almost doubling the current programme.

Announcing the long-awaited deal, Naidoo said the U.S.-Malaysian bid -- the only one to make it to the final selection stage -- had exceeded the government's three key evaluation criteria of high roll-out, training and price.

The SBC-Telekom Malaysia consortium will have five of 15 board positions following the privatisation deal and 75 expatriate staff will take a hands-on role in managing the company during the five-year exclusivity period, Naidoo said.
Jim Myers, SBC regional officer, said his company believed strongly in the South African government's goals for extending services to its people.
"We look forward to being an integral part of that process," he said.
Foreign exchange dealers said the deal would lift foreign exchange reserves, currently standing at around $2.8 billion, and should bolster the rand.
Economists applauded the sell-off which they said demonstrated a commitment by President Nelson Mandela's government to curb government borrowing and pursue market-oriented reforms.

"South Africa has been behind the curve on privatisation. For foreign investors this deal is a very important signal because once the process starts you know there is more to come," said Constantin Vayenas, an economist at UBS in London.
